analysis.one_liner: Strips injured people's right to sue insurers that fail to pay before Medicare.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee referral in the Senate and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: When Medicare is the backup payer for someone with private insurance, current law lets that person sue any primary insurer — a group health plan, a workers' compensation plan, an auto or liability plan, or a no-fault plan — that refuses to pay what it owes first, and win damages. The RAMP Act would keep that right only against employer group health plans. Workers' compensation insurers, auto insurers, liability insurers, and no-fault insurers would no longer face these suits, leaving the federal Medicare program to chase them administratively instead.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers' compensation, auto, liability, and no-fault insurance companies, who would gain protection from double-damage private lawsuits when they fail to make primary payment before Medicare steps in. The federal government retains its own administrative recovery power, so the insurers' exposure shrinks but does not vanish.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers' comp, auto, and liability insurers

how_it_helps.text: Current law allows a private right of action against any primary plan — group health, workers' compensation, automobile or liability, or no-fault — that fails to provide appropriate primary payment when Medicare is the secondary payer [S2].
The bill amends the Social Security Act to replace "primary plan" with "group health plan" in that provision, narrowing the private cause of action to group health plans only [S2] [S3].
Workers' compensation, auto, liability, and no-fault insurers would therefore no longer face damage suits from individuals over MSP payment failures, shrinking their litigation exposure [S2].

analysis.who_pays: People injured on the job or in accidents, whose workers' compensation, auto, liability, or no-fault insurers would face one fewer legal penalty for failing to pay first — and, indirectly, the Medicare program, which otherwise must pay when a primary plan does not and recoup through slower administrative channels.
analysis.who_pays_short: Injured people and the Medicare program

drawbacks.text: Limiting the private right of action removes a legal deterrent aimed at insurers who delay or refuse primary payment, leaving individuals in workers' compensation and accident cases without a private enforcement tool [S2].

If primary insurers pay less reliably, Medicare steps in more often, and the program must recover those costs administratively — a slower and less effective mechanism than a private damages action [S2].

Supporters would argue that private MSP suits, which carry double damages, push up litigation and settlement costs in workers' comp and liability claims, ultimately raising premiums; the bill is a targeted fix for that concern, but it accomplishes it by taking away enforcement from the people the suits were designed to protect [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill reduces litigation exposure for several insurance lines, which supporters argue lowers premiums, but the cost is a weakened enforcement mechanism for people whose insurers fail to pay first and a larger burden shifted onto Medicare's administrative recovery process. On balance it trades a private enforcement right for insurer protection, with the public side bearing the downside.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on May 16, 2023, and no further action was ever taken; it died when that Congress ended in January 2025 [S1] [S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Tim Scott (R-SC) introduced the RAMP Act on May 16, 2023, joined by one Democratic cosponsor [S1] [S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that was the bill's last action of record [S5].
The Finance Committee never took up the bill, and it received no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured people and the Medicare program come out ahead in the narrow sense that the private right of action against non-group-health primary plans remains intact — at least until a future Congress takes the issue up again. No one gained the litigation relief the bill would have given insurers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers gained nothing; status quo held

for.name: Sen. Tim Scott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on May 16, 2023.

for.name: Sen. Maggie Hassan
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it bipartisan at introduction.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no action on it for the remainder of the Congress — no markup, no vote, no report.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan at introduction — a Republican sponsor with one Democratic cosponsor — but it never reached a vote, so no partisan pattern can be read from the record.

industries.industry: Workers' compensation, auto, liability, and no-fault insurers
industries.note: The bill would exempt these insurers from the private damages right that exists when they fail to pay as the primary payer before Medicare, cutting their litigation exposure. The gain comes at the expense of enforcement power held by the people those insurers owe payments to.
Group health plans remain the only insurers still exposed to the private right of action after the bill's amendment, so relative to the other lines they keep the liability everyone else sheds.
Weakened private enforcement means more cases where a primary plan does not pay and Medicare covers the bill first, relying on slower administrative recovery instead of a damages action.
